transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-22
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SRE), Hannah (Redwood CSM); Tara (ClearPath ML), Devon (ClearPath Platform), Alex (CTO), Samira (ClearPath SRE)

Summary: Quick POC check-in focused on last week's stability incidents (timeouts, intermittent 5xxs during burst traffic), discussion of observed failure patterns, root-cause hypotheses, short-term mitigations (adaptive retries, backoff, rate limit tuning) and plan for a dedicated benchmark on reserved capacity. Action items defined and next steps for log sharing and runbook updates.

Topics:
- Incident recap and timeline
- Telemetry gaps and what logs to share
- Retry / backoff policy tuning and client-side knobs
- Rate limit and concurrency controls (per-tenant vs global)
- Dedicated capacity pilot & benchmark plan
- Compliance / audit concerns for log sharing

Transcript:
00:00 Jared: Thanks everyone for joining, we'll do a quick 50 minute sync. I'm Jared from Redwood, this is Priya and Marco who are on the infra side. We want to walk through the incident from last Wednesday, and set immediate mitigations plus a plan for the Dedicated pilot benchmark.
00:14 Tara: Hi all, Tara here. Quick context — we ran a daytime A/B experiment and saw a spike for about 18 minutes where a subset of requests started timing out, then a flurry of 5xxs from the API. Impact was our user-facing inference endpoint.
00:27 Devon: The traffic pattern was a burst, roughly 3x normal QPS. We were using the hosted endpoints with default concurrency. We didn't hit any client side retries initially because we were worried about duplicate UX impressions.
00:41 Priya: Ok, thanks. Can you confirm whether those timeouts were bounded to long-response requests (like 16k token runs) or short ones?
00:46 Samira: Most were 256-512 token prompts, not long-context. That's why it felt odd, we expected short requests to be fine.
00:56 Priya: Hmm, that points away from sequence-length-driven kernel slowdowns. Marco, on the infra side, what do we think — batching backlog or KV cache evictions?
01:07 Marco: Early look at runtime metrics shows CPU/GPU utilization spiked but not saturated. What we did see was a sudden doubling in request queue latency and then service worker restarts in the same window. The restarts line up with an internal healthcheck TTL causing aggressive restart loops — some memory fragmentation suspected. The worker restarts mean transient 5xxs while new processes start up.
01:28 Alex: Could that be a model OOM or a bad quant path? We had half the pilot using a quantized variant.
01:34 Priya: We noted some noisy kernels for quantized dispatch on that hardware profile. Not full OOM, but slow wake-up due to JIT/compilation on first use. Compilations can stall if the kernel selection path is hit under pressure.
01:49 Tara: That sounds plausible — the burst was timed with a deploy? I think we pushed a config change earlier that day.
01:55 Devon: Yes we had a minor config flip (cache TTLs) before the experiment. Could be correlated.
02:01 Jared: Alright we'll treat that as a hypothesis: (1) transient worker restarts and kernel compilation stalls coincident with burst traffic; (2) memory fragmentation causing healthchecks to restart workers. We'll need logs to confirm.
02:12 Priya: For immediate mitigation, we recommend three things: shorter client-side retries with jittered exponential backoff (avoid tight loops), a soft concurrency cap at the client to smooth bursts, and enable our adaptive prefix cache for hot prompts.
02:25 Samira: On retries, we were conservative; our client retries were basically disabled. We can add 2 retries with 200-600ms jitter.
02:33 Priya: That should help. Also set a request concurrency limit per worker pool to prevent the queue from backing up and triggering healthcheck restarts.
02:42 Devon: How about server-side rate limits? We saw a few 429s before the 5xx spike. Are those from global throttles?
02:50 Marco: Those 429s were from our autoscaler protection layer — when it hit headroom constraints it started returning soft-429s. In many cases the traffic pattern was bursty and the adaptive batching couldn't warm fast enough.
03:04 Jared: To be clear, backpressure can show as 429 then escalate to 5xx if workers die. So the chain matters.
03:11 Alex: For the POC, do you recommend switching to Dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors / warm pools?
03:18 Priya: Yes, Dedicated will give you reserved worker pools, warm caches, and faster kernel warm-up — it reduces variance. But there's cost tradeoffs. We also can do a focused benchmark on Dedicated to quantify tail latency improvement.
03:30 Tara: Cost is a factor. We want to see the delta before committing.
03:34 Jared: We'll run a 2-hour Dedicated benchmark with your traffic replay and share the cost estimate.
03:40 Devon: Great. What logs do you need from our side to nail root cause?
03:44 Priya: Request ids from the incident window (timestamps), the full request payloads if possible (or sanitized examples), and any agent logs showing the client side concurrency during the spike. On our side we need runtime worker logs, healthcheck traces, and kernel compilation traces.
03:57 Samira: Exporting request ids is fine; we'll sanitize payloads and send. Concern: do you need raw payloads? We have PII in some.
04:04 Jared: Sanitize or hashed payloads are fine; we just need seeds to reproduce request shapes. We'll sign an NDA addendum if needed for more detailed artifacts.
04:12 Hannah: Also to note on compliance, we can limit logs to metadata (request size, tokens, model variant, timing) if payloads are sensitive.
04:20 Tara: Ok we'll do metadata first and follow up with examples under NDA if required.
04:25 Priya: Another quick telemetry gap — can you include the headroom signal from your autoscaler? It helps us see whether scaling laged the pool.
04:32 Devon: We'll pull that.
04:35 Jared: Let's define the short-term mitigations: 1) customer enables two retries with jitter; 2) set client concurrency cap to X (TBD) for the next 48 hours; 3) Redwood to throttle kernel JIT by pre-warming on a canary stream during your off-peak.
04:50 Tara: We'll implement the retries and concurrency cap today.
04:55 Priya: For the pre-warm, we'll run a warm-up with the quantized variants and priority cache seeding. That should reduce JIT stalls. We'll coordinate a warm-up window.
05:06 Samira: If worker restarts are due to memory fragmentation, is there an immediate patch?
05:10 Marco: We can adjust healthcheck thresholds temporarily to avoid aggressive restarts, and increase worker memory headroom. That's a short-term config change. Medium term we want to root-cause the fragmentation pattern.
05:22 Alex: Any risk adjusting healthchecks? Could that hide a real OOM?
05:27 Priya: We'll only increase thresholds modestly and monitor OOM counters. If OOMs spike we'll roll back. It's about avoiding thrash while we investigate.
05:36 Tara: Sounds reasonable.
05:40 Jared: On rate limits, do you want per-tenant or per-api-key throttles?
05:45 Devon: Per-tenant probably makes more sense for our multi-tenant architecture.
05:48 Marco: Redwood supports both. For your case, per-tenant soft-429s plus a queue-based shaping layer works well — it lets critical requests through and sheds load gracefully.
05:59 Priya: Another note: enable adaptive prefix caching for hot prompts, that will reduce processing load on identical prefix sequences. We can also suggest batching-friendly client hints so the runtime batches better.
06:12 Tara: We'll try to identify hot prompts. Our A/B test uses a limited prompt set so that could be high-yield.
06:18 Jared: Good. Now planning for the Dedicated benchmark: we want your traffic replay dump (sanitized), target model and quant profile, and the 2-hour window. We'll run with both hosted and Dedicated under the same replay and show tail-latency, 95/99, and error rates.
06:33 Devon: Timeline?
06:35 Jared: If you can send artifacts by Wednesday (06-24), we can schedule the benchmark next week (say 06-29). Priya and Marco will run it and deliver a findings doc.
06:45 Tara: Works for us.
06:48 Samira: One more question: on retries, do you have recommended idempotency guidance? We're worried about duplicate inference side-effects.
06:55 Priya: Best practice is to make generation calls idempotent by using client-side dedupe keys when you can, or set low max retries with jitter. Also use a cache-key for repeated prompts. We'll share a short doc with exact headers and patterns.
07:10 Jared: We'll send that guidance and a sample client snippet.
07:15 Alex: Regarding SLA and errors, what's Redwood's visibility into audit logs for these incident windows? We need that for our compliance team.
07:21 Hannah: We can provide audit logs with request ids and timestamps; for higher retention or on-prem collection we have Private deployment options. But for the pilot we can push a daily audit extract.
07:33 Alex: Ok, we'll evaluate.
07:36 Priya: Quick heads up on cost — Dedicated reduces variance but has a minimum reserved capacity. We'll include an estimated monthly cost post-benchmark so you can evaluate ROI.
07:48 Tara: Good.
07:50 Jared: Before we wrap, any outstanding blockers?
07:52 Samira: No blockers — we'll send request ids and headroom signals by tomorrow.
07:57 Devon: We'll also check our deploy window notes to see if the config flip coincided.
08:01 Jared: Great. Recap of action items and owners captured in the notes.
08:06 Priya: We'll prepare the kernel JIT traces and pre-warm plan; Marco will propose a safe healthcheck threshold and memory headroom tweak for trial.
08:15 Jared: And I'll send the pricing note for the Dedicated run and the runbook with immediate retry/concurrency guidance.
08:22 Tara: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.
08:25 Jared: Thanks, we'll follow up with the logs link and schedule the benchmark once we have artifacts.
08:30 Meeting end.

Notes about transcript quality: Some speaker labels are humanified, others approximate; occasional overlap and filler words preserved. There are a few mis-hearings in kernel/JIT naming ("quant path" written sometimes as "quantized path") and KV cache spelled variably (KV cache, K-V cache, KVcash) — left to preserve transcription realism.

References / Links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/docs/pilot-runbook (runbook and retry guidance), internal benchmark spreadsheet link shared after call (internal link omitted in transcript), security artifacts: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2_summary.pdf

End of transcript.
